questions.q: A file has a missing ) on line 3. Line 1 is console.log("Starting");. What happens when you run it with Node.js?
questions.explain: Node.js checks the whole file before it runs any of it. A syntax error stops everything, even the lines above the mistake.
options: Line 1 prints, then the program stops at line 3
Nothing prints: Node.js reads the whole file first and stops with a SyntaxError
Node.js skips line 3 and runs the rest
It runs, but gives a wrong answer

questions.q: What is a runtime error?
questions.explain: A runtime error happens while the code runs. Everything before it has run; nothing after it runs unless the error is caught.
options: Code that is not valid JavaScript
An impossible operation while the program runs, such as reading a property of undefined
Code that runs but gives a wrong result
A warning that the program is slow

questions.q: Why does the lesson call a logic error the worst kind?
questions.explain: JavaScript cannot know what you meant, so a wrong + 1 gives a wrong answer silently. Logic errors are found by checking results against known answers: tests.
options: It prints a very long stack trace
The code runs without complaint and gives a wrong result, so nothing warns you
It can only be fixed by restarting Node.js

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The typo lenght gives undefined, and calling toFixed on undefined throws a TypeError. The line "after" never runs.

questions.q: This function should return the average priority. What does it print?
questions.explain: The average of 2 and 4 is 3, but a stray + 1 makes it 4. No error, no warning: that is a logic error.

questions.q: What does throw do?
questions.explain: throw jumps to the nearest catch: in the same function if the throw is inside a try there, otherwise in its caller, its caller's caller, and so on. If nothing catches it, the program crashes.
options: Prints the error and continues with the next line
Stops normal execution and jumps to the nearest enclosing catch, leaving functions up the call stack until one is found
Restarts the function from the top

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The second input fails our own check, which throws a plain Error. The third is not JSON, so JSON.parse itself throws a SyntaxError. Each error is caught, so the loop carries on.

questions.q: A server handles requests in a loop. Why wrap each request in try/catch?
questions.explain: An uncaught error can stop the whole server. Catching it per request turns one failure into one error answer, and the next request is handled normally.
options: So errors are never logged anywhere
To make the code run faster
So one bad request cannot stop the server from answering the next one

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: finally runs whether try returned or threw, and it runs before the function's result reaches the caller. So "finally" prints before each result.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: finally gives the connection back in both cases: after the return and after the throw. Without it, every failed query would leak a connection.

questions.q: What belongs in a finally block?
questions.explain: finally always runs: after success, after an error, even after return. That makes it the right place for clean-up.
options: The main work of the function
A second copy of the catch code
Clean-up that must happen no matter what, like closing a file or releasing a connection
Code that should only run when there was an error

questions.q: Which built-in error do Node.js and Chrome throw when the call stack overflows?
questions.explain: RangeError is for values out of range, and for "Maximum call stack size exceeded". TypeError is for wrong types, ReferenceError for unknown names.

questions.q: Which error does JSON.parse("{oops") throw?
questions.explain: Invalid JSON is invalid syntax, so JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError. You did not write that throw: built-in functions throw too.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: RangeError is a subclass of Error, so both checks are true. name is the class name and message is only the text you passed.
options:
true true
RangeError
priority must be 1 to 5, got 9

true false
RangeError
priority must be 1 to 5, got 9

true true
Error
priority must be 1 to 5, got 9

true true
RangeError
RangeError: priority must be 1 to 5, got 9

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first line of stack is the name and the message. The lines after it are the call stack, top first.
options: TypeError: title must be a string

questions.q: Why should you never write throw "not found"?
questions.explain: JavaScript lets you throw anything, but a string carries no information about what or where. Always throw an Error or a subclass.
options: A string has no name and no stack, and instanceof cannot recognise it
It makes the program exit immediately

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: What you catch is just the string. It is not an Error, and it has no name and no stack, so the code that catches it cannot tell what happened.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The new error gives the caller a clear message at its own level. error.cause still holds the original SyntaxError from JSON.parse for debugging.

questions.q: Why pass { cause: error } when you wrap a low-level error in a new one?
questions.explain: Without cause, the original error disappears. With it, the caller reads "Could not load settings" and a developer can still see the real SyntaxError.
options: It hides the original error from developers
The clear new message goes to the caller, and the original detail is not lost
It makes the new error a SyntaxError
It is required, or new Error throws

questions.q: Why give each kind of failure its own error class, like NotFoundError and ValidationError?
questions.explain: "Task not found" should give 404, "bad input" 400, "database down" 500. Separate classes let the catching code decide with instanceof.
options: So the code that catches it can tell them apart with instanceof and answer differently
Because JavaScript limits how many plain errors you can throw
So the stack trace is shorter

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: new.target is the class new was called with, here NotFoundError, even inside the parent's constructor. It extends AppError, so instanceof AppError is true.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The second parameter defaults to {}, and status and code have their own defaults. So calling it with only a message is safe.

questions.q: A catch handles NotFoundError and ValidationError. What should it do with any other error?
questions.explain: Only handle the errors you expect. A catch that swallows everything hides real bugs. Re-throwing lets a higher level deal with it.
options: Ignore it, so the program keeps running
Re-throw it with throw error; so it keeps going up and is not silently lost

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The expected NotFoundError is handled. The TypeError from null.title is not expected, so handle re-throws it and the outer catch receives it.

questions.q: In a ZudoJS app you need a "not found" error with status 404. What should you do?
questions.explain: @zudojs/errors ships NotFoundError, ValidationError, ConflictError and many more, following the same pattern as this lesson. Use them instead of rewriting them.
options: Write your own class NotFoundError extends Error in every package
Import NotFoundError from @zudojs/errors, which already has the right status
Return null and let the caller guess

questions.q: In the calculator API, which status code does a=10&b=0&op=divide get, and why?
questions.explain: The input is valid, so it is not 400. The calculator throws its own DivisionByZeroError with status 422: "I understood, but I cannot do it".
options: 422, because the request is well formed but the calculation cannot be done
500, because dividing by zero crashes the server

questions.q: Why does the calculator look up op in an OPERATIONS allow-list instead of using eval?
questions.explain: User input must never be run as code. An allow-list only accepts the operations you wrote, and everything else is refused with a ValidationError.
options: eval would run whatever the user typed as code on your server
Objects are easier to read than strings

questions.q: Why does the calculator use Object.hasOwn? What does this print?
questions.explain: Every object inherits constructor from Object.prototype, so a plain lookup finds it. Object.hasOwn only accepts keys you wrote yourself, so op=constructor is refused.

questions.q: URL values arrive as strings. What does this print?
questions.explain: Empty text is checked first, because Number(" ") would silently give 0. "ten" becomes NaN, which is not finite. A missing value is not a string at all.
options: 10 a is required b must be a number b is required
10 0 b must be a number b is required
10 a is required NaN b is required
10 a is required b must be a number b must be a number

questions.q: The API catches an error that is not an AppError, such as an unexpected TypeError. What should it send the client?
questions.explain: An unexpected error's message and stack can reveal file paths, library versions, SQL or data, which attackers collect. Log them privately and answer with a generic message.
options: The error's message and stack, so the client can report the bug
A generic 500 "Something went wrong", and log the real details where only developers can read them
A 400, because the client must have sent something wrong
Nothing: let the server crash so someone notices

questions.q: Which error message is safe to send to the client as it is?
questions.explain: Errors you designed for users, like ValidationError, contain only what you chose to say. Everything unexpected gets the generic 500 message.
options: The message of an unexpected TypeError inside the calculator
The stack trace of any error
The message of a ValidationError you designed for users, like "a must be a number"
The message of a database error

questions.q: In the calculator build, which part knows about HTTP status codes in responses?
questions.explain: The calculator only validates, calculates and throws typed errors. The API layer is the single place that maps them to a status and body. A new error type then fits in without changing the calculator's callers.
options: Only the API layer, handleCalculate, which turns errors into responses
Every function, so each can answer the client

questions.q: A small version of the API layer. What does this print?
questions.explain: Known AppErrors keep their status and message. The TypeError from null.a is unexpected, so the client only gets a generic 500 message.
options: 200 400 a is required 500 Something went wrong
200 400 a is required 400 Something went wrong
200 500 a is required 500 Something went wrong
200 400 a is required 500 Cannot read properties of null (reading 'a')

questions.q: This function should return null only for invalid JSON. What does it print?
questions.explain: The third input is valid JSON without a title, so toUpperCase throws a TypeError. The catch catches every error and hides that bug behind null. Only catch what you expect.

questions.q: Write ConflictError extends AppError with status 409 and code "CONFLICT". Then make createUser throw it with the message "<email> is already registered" when the e-mail is taken. The program should print 409 ConflictError ada@example.com is already registered.
questions.explain: The subclass passes its status and code to super; new.target.name in the base class sets the name. users.some(...) checks whether the e-mail is taken.

questions.q: Fix readTitle so only a SyntaxError from JSON.parse becomes null. Any other error must be re-thrown. The program should print BUY MILK, null, then TypeError.
questions.explain: Put only the line that may throw the expected error inside try, check instanceof SyntaxError, and re-throw anything else. The missing title now shows up as a real error instead of hiding behind null.

questions.q: Finish withConnection(work): add 1 to open, run work() and return its result, and make sure open goes back down by 1 even when work throws. Use finally. The program should print rows, failed: timeout, open: 0.
questions.explain: try { return work(); } finally { open -= 1; } releases the connection after a return and after a throw. No catch is needed: the error still goes up to the caller.

questions.q: Finish loadConfig(text): return the parsed JSON, but when parsing fails, throw a new Error("Could not load config") with the original error as its cause. The program should print Could not load config and then SyntaxError.
questions.explain: new Error(message, { cause: error }) gives a clear message at your level and keeps the original SyntaxError for debugging.

questions.q: Finish power(a, b): throw new ValidationError("b must be at most 100", "b") when b is larger than 100, otherwise return a ** b. The program should print 1024 and then 400 field b: b must be at most 100.
questions.explain: Limiting the exponent stops anyone from asking the server for huge numbers. Because it is a ValidationError, the API answers 400 without any change to the API layer.
questions.expected:
1024
400 field b: b must be at most 100

questions.q: Finish toResponse(error). For an AppError, return { status: error.status, message: error.message }. For any other error, return { status: 500, message: "Something went wrong" } so internal details never reach the client. The program should print 404 Task 7 not found and then 500 Something went wrong.
questions.explain: Only errors you designed for users are shown as they are. The TypeError message reveals internals (here, that a password field exists), so the client gets the generic text.
questions.expected:
404 Task 7 not found
500 Something went wrong

questions.q: Finish calculate(op, a, b). Look op up in OPERATIONS with Object.hasOwn; if it is not there, throw new Error(`unknown operation "${op}"`). The program should print 7, then unknown operation "constructor".
questions.explain: OPERATIONS["constructor"] exists through the prototype chain. Object.hasOwn accepts only the operations you wrote, so inherited names are refused.

questions.q: Finish toNumber(value, field). Throw new Error(`${field} is required`) when the value is not a string or is empty after trimming, and new Error(`${field} must be a number`) when Number(value) is not finite. Otherwise return the number. The program should print 10, a is required, b must be a number.
questions.explain: Check for empty text first, because Number(" ") is 0. Number.isFinite then rejects NaN and Infinity.
questions.expected:
10
a is required
b must be a number
